claim: Signalling pathways leading to post-synaptic plasticity have been examined in many types of experimental studies.
source: Signalling pathways leading to post-synaptic plasticity have been examined in many types of experimental studies, but a unified picture on how multiple biochemical pathways collectively shape neocortical plasticity is missing.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field, representing established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: A unified picture on how multiple biochemical pathways collectively shape neocortical plasticity is missing.
source: Signalling pathways leading to post-synaptic plasticity have been examined in many types of experimental studies, but a unified picture on how multiple biochemical pathways collectively shape neocortical plasticity is missing.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in current knowledge, based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: The authors built a biochemically detailed model of post-synaptic plasticity describing CaMKII, PKA, and PKC pathways and their contribution to synaptic potentiation or depression.
source: We built a biochemically detailed model of post-synaptic plasticity describing CaMKII, PKA, and PKC pathways and their contribution to synaptic potentiation or depression.
evidence: This is a direct statement of what the authors did in this work.

claim: The authors developed a statistical AMPA-receptor-tetramer model that permits the estimation of the AMPA-receptor-mediated maximal synaptic conductance based on numbers of GluR1s and GluR2s predicted by the biochemical signalling model.
source: We developed a statistical AMPA-receptor-tetramer model, which permits the estimation of the AMPA-receptor-mediated maximal synaptic conductance based on numbers of GluR1s and GluR2s predicted by the biochemical signalling model.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a methodological contribution of the work.

claim: The model reproduces neuromodulator-gated spike-timing-dependent plasticity as observed in the visual cortex.
source: We show that our model reproduces neuromodulator-gated spike-timing-dependent plasticity as observed in the visual cortex and can be fit to data from many cortical areas, uncovering the biochemical contributions of the pathways pinpointed by the underlying experimental studies.
evidence: This is a claim about the model's ability to reproduce experimental observations, supported by the simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The model can be fit to data from many cortical areas, uncovering the biochemical contributions of the pathways pinpointed by the underlying experimental studies.
source: We show that our model reproduces neuromodulator-gated spike-timing-dependent plasticity as observed in the visual cortex and can be fit to data from many cortical areas, uncovering the biochemical contributions of the pathways pinpointed by the underlying experimental studies.
evidence: This is supported by the model fitting experiments described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 9.

claim: The model explains the dependence of different forms of plasticity on the availability of different proteins.
source: Our model explains the dependence of different forms of plasticity on the availability of different proteins and can be used for the study of mental disorder-associated impairments of cortical plasticity.
evidence: This is supported by the parameter variation experiments shown in Figure 7 and related analyses.

claim: The model can be used for the study of mental disorder-associated impairments of cortical plasticity.
source: Our model explains the dependence of different forms of plasticity on the availability of different proteins and can be used for the study of mental disorder-associated impairments of cortical plasticity.
evidence: This is a prospective claim about potential applications of the model.

claim: Neocortical long-term potentiation (LTP) was first observed by Komatsu et al., 1981 and Lee, 1982.
source: Synaptic plasticity in the neocortex has been under intense research since the first observations of neocortical long-term potentiation (LTP) (Komatsu et al., 1981; Lee, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original studies.

claim: Synaptic plasticity in the neocortex is a key phenomenon underlying vital mammalian brain processes ranging from formation and storage of memories to attentional selection.
source: Although most often studied in brain slices, synaptic plasticity in the neocortex is a key phenomenon underlying vital mammalian brain processes ranging from formation and storage of memories to attentional selection (Roelfsema and Holtmaat, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Cortical plasticity processes are impaired in heritable mental illnesses such as schizophrenia and fragile X syndrome, as well as neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease.
source: These processes are impaired in heritable mental illnesses such as schizophrenia and fragile X syndrome, as well as neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, all of which have been associated with deficits in cortical plasticity (Kantrowitz et al., 2017; Martin and Huntsman, 2012; Koch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on these disorders.

claim: Schizophrenia, fragile X syndrome, and Alzheimer's disease have been associated with deficits in cortical plasticity.
source: These processes are impaired in heritable mental illnesses such as schizophrenia and fragile X syndrome, as well as neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, all of which have been associated with deficits in cortical plasticity (Kantrowitz et al., 2017; Martin and Huntsman, 2012; Koch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to relevant studies.

claim: Synaptic plasticity in the neocortex is highly variable, with outcomes depending on the cortical area, neuron type, and details of the stimulation protocol.
source: Similar to hippocampal synaptic plasticity (Larkman and Jack, 1995), synaptic plasticity in the neocortex is highly variable — the outcomes of any plasticity-inducing protocol depends on the cortical area, neuron type as well as details of the stimulation protocol (Castro-Alamancos et al., 1995; Froc and Racine, 2005; Sjöström et al., 2008; Feldman, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The BCM theory predicts that small synaptic activity (small Ca2+ transients) cause long-term depression (LTD) whereas large synaptic activity (large Ca2+ transients) give rise to LTP.
source: The foundations of our mechanistic understanding of neocortical synaptic plasticity lie upon the phenomenological Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro (BCM) theory, which predicts that small synaptic activity (later attributed to small Ca2+ transients [Bear et al., 1987; Lisman, 1989]) cause long-term depression (LTD) whereas large synaptic activity (large Ca2+ transients) give rise to LTP (Bienenstock et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original BCM theory and subsequent work.

claim: Simple BCM-based models and related models of spike-timing-dependent plasticity typically fail to provide a mechanistic understanding of the biochemistry within the synapse.
source: These models, however, typically fail to provide a mechanistic understanding of the biochemistry within the synapse — namely, they do not reveal how various molecules downstream of Ca2+ regulate the induction and maintenance of plasticity occurring in neuronal circuits, their composite neurons and synapses of the cortex.
evidence: This is an assessment of limitations of existing models based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: Current models often ignore the joint contributions of neuromodulators, which are critical for inducing some forms of cortical synaptic plasticity.
source: Moreover, current models often ignore the joint contributions of neuromodulators, which are critical for inducing some forms of cortical synaptic plasticity (Meunier et al., 2017; Brzosko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on neuromodulator-dependent plasticity.

claim: Models of intracellular signalling have been used to study LTP and LTD in the hippocampus.
source: Despite the lack of biochemically detailed models of synaptic plasticity in the neocortex, models of intracellular signalling have been used to study LTP and LTD in the hippocampus (Bhalla and Iyengar, 1999; Jȩdrzejewska-Szmek et al., 2017), cerebellum (Gallimore et al., 2018), and striatum (Blackwell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: Models of intracellular signalling have been used to study LTP and LTD in the cerebellum.
source: Despite the lack of biochemically detailed models of synaptic plasticity in the neocortex, models of intracellular signalling have been used to study LTP and LTD in the hippocampus (Bhalla and Iyengar, 1999; Jȩdrzejewska-Szmek et al., 2017), cerebellum (Gallimore et al., 2018), and striatum (Blackwell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a modeling study.

claim: Models of intracellular signalling have been used to study LTP and LTD in the striatum.
source: Despite the lack of biochemically detailed models of synaptic plasticity in the neocortex, models of intracellular signalling have been used to study LTP and LTD in the hippocampus (Bhalla and Iyengar, 1999; Jȩdrzejewska-Szmek et al., 2017), cerebellum (Gallimore et al., 2018), and striatum (Blackwell et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a modeling study.

claim: The authors' model is based on the model of Jȩdrzejewska-Szmek et al., 2017, which describes the PKA- and CaMKII-dependent phosphorylation of AMPAR subunit 1 (GluR1).
source: In short, we based our model on that of Jȩdrzejewska-Szmek et al., 2017, which describes the PKA- and CaMKII-dependent phosphorylation of AMPAR subunit 1 (GluR1), and added the metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR) and muscarinic acetylcholine M1 receptor-mediated activation of PKC from Kim et al., 2013 and Blackwell et al., 2019, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model construction methodology.

claim: The authors added the metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR) and muscarinic acetylcholine M1 receptor-mediated activation of PKC from Kim et al., 2013 and Blackwell et al., 2019.
source: In short, we based our model on that of Jȩdrzejewska-Szmek et al., 2017, which describes the PKA- and CaMKII-dependent phosphorylation of AMPAR subunit 1 (GluR1), and added the metabotropic glutamate receptor (mGluR) and muscarinic acetylcholine M1 receptor-mediated activation of PKC from Kim et al., 2013 and Blackwell et al., 2019, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model construction methodology with citations.

claim: The authors adopted the reactions describing PKC-dependent phosphorylation and endocytosis of AMPAR subunit 2 (GluR2) and reinsertion to the membrane from Gallimore et al., 2018.
source: We then adopted the reactions describing PKC-dependent phosphorylation and endocytosis of AMPAR subunit 2 (GluR2) and reinsertion to the membrane from Gallimore et al., 2018, which allowed the representation of post-synaptic depression with our model.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model construction methodology with citation.

claim: CaMKII is required for esophageal acid-induced sensitisation in cingulate cortex.
source: CaMKII	Cingulate cortex	Esophageal acid-induced sensitisation	post-syn.	Banerjee et al., 2013
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study, as shown in Table 1A.

claim: CaMKII is required for 5-HT1-induced modulation of AMPA currents in prefrontal cortex pyramidal neurons.
source: CaMKII	Prefrontal cortex, pyramidal neurons	5-HT1-induced modulation of AMPA currents	post-syn.	Cai et al., 2002
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study, as shown in Table 1A.

claim: β-adrenergic receptors and PKA are required for potentiation of AMPA currents in visual cortex layer 4 pyramidal cells.
source: β-adr. receptors, PKA	Visual cortex, layer 4 pyramidal cells	Potentiation of AMPA currents	post-syn.	Seol et al., 2007
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study, as shown in Table 1A.

claim: M1 receptors and PKC are required for depression of AMPA currents in visual cortex layer 4 pyramidal cells.
source: M1 receptors, PKC	Visual cortex, layer 4 pyramidal cells	Depression of AMPA currents	post-syn.	Seol et al., 2007
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study, as shown in Table 1A.

claim: PKC is required for internalisation of AMPARs in cultured cortical neurons.
source: PKC	Cultured cortical neurons	Internalisation of AMPARs	post-syn.	Chung et al., 2000
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study, as shown in Table 1A.

claim: The injected Ca2+ quickly bound to Ca2+ buffers (immobile buffer and calbindin) with a 95% saturation reached in 1–2 s.
source: The injected Ca2+ quickly bound to Ca2+ buffers (immobile buffer and calbindin, Figure 2B) and pumps (PMCA and NCX, Figure 2C) as well as to the proteins of the PKC pathway (phospholipase A2 (PLA2) and C (PLC), Figure 2D): a 95% saturation was reached in 1–2 s (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: The activation of calmodulin (CaM) was slower than the binding of Ca2+ to buffers and pumps, with a 95% saturation reached in 32–53 s.
source: In contrast, the activation of calmodulin (CaM) was slower (Figure 2E): a 95% saturation was reached in 32–53 s, depending on the magnitude of the Ca2+ input.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A vast majority of Ca2+ was quickly bound and only a small fraction remained free in the cytosol.
source: Consistent with experimental literature, a vast majority of Ca2+ was quickly bound and only a small fraction remained free in the cytosol (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2F and is consistent with experimental knowledge.

claim: DGL was most completely activated throughout the Ca2+ amplitude range, owing to the large equilibrium constant of its Ca2+ binding.
source: DGL was most completely activated throughout the Ca2+ amplitude, owing to the large equilibrium constant of its Ca2+ binding.
evidence: This is based on the simulation results shown in Figure 2G and the model parameters.

claim: At extremely large Ca2+ fluxes, CaM was more completely bound by Ca2+ than PLC and PLA2.
source: At extremely large Ca2+ fluxes, CaM was more completely bound by Ca2+ than PLC and PLA2 (Figure 2G), but at lower Ca2+ amplitudes, CaM remained largely unbound (Figure 2G inset).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2G.

claim: At lower Ca2+ amplitudes, CaM remained largely unbound.
source: At extremely large Ca2+ fluxes, CaM was more completely bound by Ca2+ than PLC and PLA2 (Figure 2G), but at lower Ca2+ amplitudes, CaM remained largely unbound (Figure 2G inset).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2G inset.

claim: The PKC pathway was dependent on the cholinergic ligands or the activation of the mGluRs.
source: PKC, by contrast, became activated at relatively small Ca2+ amplitudes (Figure 2J). Of these three pathways, the PKC pathway was dependent on the cholinergic ligands or the activation of the mGluRs (Figure 2J), and the PKA pathway was dependent on the availability of β-adrenergic ligands (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The PKA pathway was dependent on the availability of β-adrenergic ligands.
source: PKC, by contrast, became activated at relatively small Ca2+ amplitudes (Figure 2J). Of these three pathways, the PKC pathway was dependent on the cholinergic ligands or the activation of the mGluRs (Figure 2J), and the PKA pathway was dependent on the availability of β-adrenergic ligands (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Large Ca2+ flux to the post-synaptic spine is needed for the activation of the CaMKII pathway.
source: Taken together, these results highlight the need for large Ca2+ flux to the post-synaptic spine for the activation of the CaMKII pathway, relatively large Ca2+ flux for the activation of the PKA pathway, and relatively small Ca2+ flux for the activation of the PKC pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Relatively large Ca2+ flux is needed for the activation of the PKA pathway.
source: Taken together, these results highlight the need for large Ca2+ flux to the post-synaptic spine for the activation of the CaMKII pathway, relatively large Ca2+ flux for the activation of the PKA pathway, and relatively small Ca2+ flux for the activation of the PKC pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Relatively small Ca2+ flux is needed for the activation of the PKC pathway.
source: Taken together, these results highlight the need for large Ca2+ flux to the post-synaptic spine for the activation of the CaMKII pathway, relatively large Ca2+ flux for the activation of the PKA pathway, and relatively small Ca2+ flux for the activation of the PKC pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Phosphorylation of GluR1 subunits at S845 increases the insertion rate of the AMPAR into the membrane, leading to post-synaptic LTP.
source: Phosphorylation of GluR1 subunits at S845 increases the insertion rate of the AMPAR into the membrane, thus leading to post-synaptic LTP (Diering et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Phosphorylation of GluR2 subunits at S880 increases the rate of receptor endocytosis from the membrane and has been observed to lead to post-synaptic LTD.
source: Conversely, phosphorylation of GluR2 subunits at S880 increases the rate of receptor endocytosis from the membrane, and has thus been observed to lead to post-synaptic LTD (Xia et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: Phosphorylation at S831 of the GluR1 subunit affects the conductance of the channel.
source: However, it is not the number of the membrane-expressed AMPAR subunits alone that determine the strength of the synapse, but different compositions of the subunits have different single-channel conductances, and phosphorylation at S831 of the GluR1 subunit also affects the conductance of the channel (Oh and Derkach, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: The 4xHFS protocol causes a large increase in total synaptic conductance due to a radical increase in membrane-inserted GluR1 subunits and a decrease in GluR2 subunits.
source: In the 4xHFS protocol, which typically causes LTP in plasticity experiments, our model predicts a large increase in total synaptic conductance (Figure 3A) due to a radical increase in membrane-inserted GluR1 subunits (Figure 3B) and a decrease in GluR2 subunits (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: The LFS protocol causes a prominent (20%) decrease in total synaptic conductance due to a decrease in GluR2 subunits.
source: In the LFS protocol, which typically causes LTD in the experiments, our model predicts a prominent (20%) decrease in total synaptic conductance (Figure 3S) due to a decrease in GluR2 subunits.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3S.

claim: In the LFS protocol, the Ca2+ inputs are insufficiently large to activate CaM, and the Gs proteins remain deactivated.
source: In this protocol, the Ca2+ inputs are insufficiently large to activate CaM, and the Gs proteins remain deactivated as well (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on simulation results that are not shown in the figures.

claim: In the LFS protocol, CaMKII and PKA pathways remain deactivated, and the effect on GluR1 phosphorylation and membrane insertion is small.
source: In consequence, CaMKII and PKA pathways remain deactivated, and the effect of the LFS protocol on GluR1 phosphorylation and membrane insertion is small (Figure 3T).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3T.

claim: In the LFS protocol, the PKC pathway is almost as strongly activated as in the 4xHFS protocol, leading to prominent S880 phosphorylation of GluR2 and removal of GluR2 from the membrane.
source: By contrast, the PKC pathway is almost as strongly activated as in the 4xHFS protocol (data not shown), leading to prominent S880 phosphorylation of GluR2 (data not shown) and removal of GluR2 from the membrane (Figure 3U).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3U and data not shown.

claim: GluR1-deficient synapses failed to show 4xHFS-induced LTP.
source: The expression of both LFS-induced LTD and 4xHFS-induced LTP of these types is dependent on the presence of both GluR1 and GluR2 subunits: GluR1-deficient synapses failed to show 4xHFS-induced LTP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and GluR2-deficient synapses failed to show LFS-induced LTD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: GluR2-deficient synapses failed to show LFS-induced LTD.
source: The expression of both LFS-induced LTD and 4xHFS-induced LTP of these types is dependent on the presence of both GluR1 and GluR2 subunits: GluR1-deficient synapses failed to show 4xHFS-induced LTP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) and GluR2-deficient synapses failed to show LFS-induced LTD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The model reproduced LFS-induced LTD and 4xHFS-induced LTP using a dimer-of-like-dimers rule with a modified (35:65) balance of GluR1 vs. GluR2 subunits.
source: We reproduced the LFS-induced LTD and 4xHFS-induced LTP using this dimer-of-like-dimers rule with a modified (35:65) balance of GluR1 vs. GluR2 subunits (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The model predicted that 6xHFSt induced LTP whereas LFS-1Hz induced LTD, in accordance with experimental data from somatosensory cortex.
source: In accordance with Figure 3 and experimental data from somatosensory cortex (Heusler et al., 2000), our model predicted that 6xHFSt induced LTP whereas LFS-1Hz induced LTD (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and comparison with experimental data.

claim: Blocking Ca2+ entry completely abolished 4xHFS-induced LTP.
source: All pathways leading to GluR1 and GluR2 phosphorylation and the consequent exocytosis and endocytosis are Ca2+-dependent: blocking Ca2+ entry completely abolished 4xHFS-induced LTP (Figure 4A) that followed GluR1 insertion (Figure 4B) and GluR2 endocytosis (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Blocking β-adrenergic ligands abolished the 4xHFS-induced LTP by suppressing the membrane-insertion of GluR1, but had no effect on GluR2 endocytosis.
source: Blocking β-adrenergic ligands abolished the 4xHFS-induced LTP (Figure 4A) by suppressing the membrane-insertion of GluR1 (Figure 4B), but had no effect on GluR2 endocytosis (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Blocking β-adrenergic ligands had no effect on LFS-induced LTD.
source: Likewise, blocking β-adrenergic ligands had no effect on LFS-induced LTD (not shown).
evidence: This is based on simulation results that are not shown.

claim: LFS-induced LTD was reduced by blockade of mGluR activation.
source: In contrast, LFS-induced LTD (Figure 4E) that followed GluR2 endocytosis (Figure 4G) was reduced by blockade of mGluR activation while the number of GluR1 subunits at the membrane remained unaffected (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: The reduction of LFS-induced LTD by mGluR blockade was strengthened by simultaneous blockade of cholinergic inputs.
source: This reduction was strengthened by simultaneous blockade of cholinergic inputs (Figure 4E–G, yellow traces).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: Blocking mGluR and M1-receptor activation reduced the amplitude of the 4xHFS-induced LTP by disabling GluR2 endocytosis while it had no effect on GluR1 insertion.
source: Counterintuitively, blocking mGluR and M1-receptor activation also reduced the amplitude of the 4xHFS-induced LTP (Figure 4A) by disabling GluR2 endocytosis (Figure 4C) while it had no effect on GluR1 insertion (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: In the PKC pathway-blocked case there is a smaller post-4xHFS membrane-bound GluR1 ratio than in the control case, and thus the probability of AMPARs being homomeric GluR1 tetramers is much smaller.
source: The reason for this is that in the PKC pathway-blocked case there is a smaller post-4xHFS membrane-bound GluR1 ratio (fraction of GluR1 subunits over all GluR subunits at the membrane) than in the control case, and thus the probability of AMPARs being homomeric GluR1 tetramers (which had a very large conductance compared to other tetramers; Equation 5) is much smaller in the former case than in control (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is an explanation based on the simulation results shown in Figure 4D and the model equations.

claim: The model reproduced the observation that paired synaptic-somatic stimulation led to little change in predicted synaptic conductance in the absence of β-adrenergic and cholinergic neuromodulation.
source: Our model predicted that there is little change in the membrane expression of GluR1 and GluR2 type receptor subunits in this stimulation protocol (Figure 5H–I, purple). Consequently, our model reproduced the observation (Seol et al., 2007) that this stimulation protocol led to little change in predicted synaptic conductance (Figure 5J, purple).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5H-J and comparison with experimental data.

claim: In the presence of β-adrenergic ligand, the model predicted a prominent (up to 70%) increase in GluR1 membrane expression with little effect on GluR2 membrane expression.
source: We next considered the paired synaptic-somatic stimulation in the presence of β-adrenergic ligand. Our model predicted a prominent (up to 70%) increase in GluR1 membrane expression with little effect on GluR2 membrane expression (Figure 5H–I, blue).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5H-I.

claim: The predicted increase in GluR1 membrane expression and synaptic conductance were most prominent when the ISI was around 20–80 ms, and modest for large ISIs.
source: The predicted increase in GluR1 membrane expression (Figure 5H) and the consequent increase in synaptic conductance (Figure 5J, blue) were most prominent when the ISI was around 20–80 ms, and modest for large ISIs.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5H and 5J.

claim: The model predictions of ISI-dependent potentiation of the EPSCs in the presence of β-adrenergic receptor agonists and absence of cholinergic agonists are consistent with experiments.
source: These predictions are consistent with the experiments where an ISI-dependent potentiation of the EPSCs in the presence of β-adrenergic receptor agonists and absence of cholinergic agonists was observed (Seol et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a comparison of model predictions with experimental data.

claim: When β-adrenergic neurotransmission was blocked but M1 receptors were activated by cholinergic ligands, the model predicted a prominent (up to 60%) decrease in GluR2 membrane expression, with little effect on GluR1 membrane expression.
source: When β-adrenergic neurotransmission was blocked but M1 receptors were activated by cholinergic ligands, the model predicted a prominent (up to 60%) decrease in GluR2 membrane expression, with little effect on GluR1 membrane expression (Figure 5K–L, purple).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5K-L.

claim: The model predicted a decrease in total conductance in a GluR1-GluR2-balanced synapse when β-adrenergic neurotransmission was blocked but M1 receptors were activated, which is in line with experimental data.
source: Our model of synaptic conductance (Equation 5) predicted a decrease in total conductance in a GluR1-GluR2-balanced synapse for this condition (Figure 5M, purple), which is in line with the experimental data (Seol et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5M and comparison with experimental data.

claim: When both β-adrenergic and cholinergic neurotransmission were active, the model predicted an increased GluR1 membrane expression and decreased GluR2 membrane expression, both of which were ISI dependent.
source: Finally, when both β-adrenergic and cholinergic neurotransmission were active, our model predicted an increased GluR1 membrane expression and decreased GluR2 membrane expression, both of which were ISI dependent (Figure 5K–L, blue).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5K-L.

claim: In simulations with both β-adrenergic and cholinergic neurotransmission, the predicted synaptic conductance was increased for small and moderate pre-post intervals and decreased otherwise, which is qualitatively similar to experimental data.
source: In these simulations, the predicted synaptic conductance was increased for small and moderate pre-post intervals and decreased otherwise (Figure 5M, blue), which is qualitatively similar to experimental data (Seol et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 5M and comparison with experimental data.

claim: In simulations where GluR1 subunits were absent, only LTD was induced by the STDP protocol.
source: These results are dependent on the availability of both GluR1 and GluR2 subunits at the post-synaptic spine: in simulations where GluR1 or GluR2 subunits were absent, only LTD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) or LTP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), respectively, was induced by the STDP protocol.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In simulations where GluR2 subunits were absent, only LTP was induced by the STDP protocol.
source: These results are dependent on the availability of both GluR1 and GluR2 subunits at the post-synaptic spine: in simulations where GluR1 or GluR2 subunits were absent, only LTD (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C) or LTP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), respectively, was induced by the STDP protocol.
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The model with balanced numbers of GluR1 and GluR2 subunits reproduces the neuromodulator-gated STDP observed in layer 2/3 pyramidal cells of the visual cortex.
source: Taken together, our model with balanced numbers of GluR1 and GluR2 subunits reproduces the neuromodulator-gated STDP observed in layer 2/3 pyramidal cells of the visual cortex.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the simulation results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Decreasing the number of spikes per burst decreases the amplitude of both LTP and LTD in the STDP protocol and brings the LTD for large post-pre ISIs close to zero.
source: Our simulations suggest that decreasing the number of spikes per burst decreases the amplitude of both LTP and LTD in the STDP protocol and, in particular, brings the LTD for large post-pre ISIs close to zero (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The larger the number of post-synaptic pulses in the pairing burst, the larger the SK currents.
source: These counter-intuitive effects can be explained by the accumulation of small-conductance K+ (SK) conductance in the post-synaptic neuron: the larger the number of post-synaptic pulses in the pairing burst, the larger the SK currents (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The SK current decays slowly (matching the Ca2+ concentration decay), and remnants of the SK currents can be observed as long as 200 ms after the post-synaptic stimulus.
source: The SK current decays slowly (matching the Ca2+ concentration decay), and remnants of the SK currents can be observed as long as 200 ms after the post-synaptic stimulus (Figure 6B inset).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 6B inset.

claim: Decreasing the SK conductance shortened the post-pre LTD window and decreased the amplitude of LTD.
source: The paired-pulse protocol of Figure 5M (involving both β-adrenergic and cholinergic neuromodulation) caused an STDP in all cases, but decreasing the SK conductance shortened the post-pre LTD window and decreased the amplitude of LTD (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The model predictions agree with the observation that the plasticity outcome is not determined by Ca2+ transient amplitude.
source: Our model predictions also agree with the observation that the plasticity outcome is not determined by Ca2+ transient amplitude (Nevian and Sakmann, 2006), instead, our model suggests that the total Ca2+ is a better predictor of the plasticity outcome: the correlation coefficient between the post-STDP synaptic conductance and the peak Ca2+ transient amplitude (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) was 0.53, while that between the post-STDP synaptic conductance and the mean Ca2+ input during the inter-stimulus interval (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1F) was 0.96 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and comparison with experimental data.

claim: The model suggests that the total Ca2+ is a better predictor of the plasticity outcome than the peak Ca2+ transient amplitude.
source: Our model predictions also agree with the observation that the plasticity outcome is not determined by Ca2+ transient amplitude (Nevian and Sakmann, 2006), instead, our model suggests that the total Ca2+ is a better predictor of the plasticity outcome: the correlation coefficient between the post-STDP synaptic conductance and the peak Ca2+ transient amplitude (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) was 0.53, while that between the post-STDP synaptic conductance and the mean Ca2+ input during the inter-stimulus interval (see Figure 5—figure supplement 1F) was 0.96 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Low GluR1 ratio was needed for strong LTD and medium or high GluR1 ratio for strong LTP.
source: Low GluR1 ratio was needed for strong LTD and medium or high GluR1 ratio for strong LTP (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by the parameter exploration results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The strongest forms of LTP (classes 11–16) were induced only when GluR1 ratio was smaller than 1.
source: However, the strongest forms of LTP (classes 11–16) were induced only when GluR1 ratio was smaller than 1 (Figure 7B), because a very low number of GluR2 subunits implied that the synapse has many homomeric GluR1 tetramers at a basal state, and thus stimulation-induced GluR1 exocytosis and GluR2 endocytosis did not radically increase the number of homomeric GluR1 tetramers (Equation 5, see also Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the parameter exploration results shown in Figure 7B and explained by the model equations.

claim: Very strong LTP (classes 10–16) required a small to medium NCX concentration and a medium to large PKA-pathway coefficient.
source: For LTD and moderate LTP (classes 1–5), any NCX concentration and PKA-pathway coefficient could be used, but very strong LTP (classes 10–16) required a small to medium NCX concentration (Figure 7C) and a medium to large PKA-pathway coefficient (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by the parameter exploration results shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: PKC-pathway coefficient alone was not predictive of plasticity outcome.
source: By contrast, PKC-pathway coefficient alone was not predictive of plasticity outcome (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by the parameter exploration results shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Moderate GluR1 ratios (0.40–0.57) and moderate NCX concentrations (0.7–1.4 times the default value) were needed for the default BCM-type plasticity.
source: Moderate GluR1 ratios (0.40–0.57; Figure 7F, black) and moderate NCX concentrations (0.7–1.4 times the default value; Figure 7F, black) were needed for the default BCM-type plasticity, while for the linear LTP curve a larger GluR1 ratio (0.59–0.92; Figure 7F, red) was needed but the NCX concentration was more variable (values ranged from 0.4 to 1.7 times the default value; Figure 7G, red).
evidence: This is supported by the parameter exploration results shown in Figure 7F-G.

claim: The PKA pathway coefficients were generally larger in the default BCM-type plasticity parameter sets than in the parameter sets producing the linear LTP curve.
source: The PKA pathway coefficients were generally larger in the default BCM-type plasticity parameter sets than in the parameter sets producing the linear LTP curve (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by the parameter exploration results shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Alterations of the concentrations of the proteins regulating Ca2+ efflux or PKA/PKC-pathway signalling and the numbers of GluR1 and GluR2 subunits have a large effect both on the type of plasticity (LTP or LTD) and on the sensitivity of the plasticity outcome to the amplitude of the Ca2+ flux.
source: Taken together, our results show that alterations of the concentrations of the proteins regulating Ca2+ efflux or PKA/PKC-pathway signalling and the numbers of GluR1 and GluR2 subunits, ranging from complete absence to moderate increase (±100%), have a large effect both on the type of plasticity (LTP or LTD) and on the sensitivity of the plasticity outcome to the amplitude of the Ca2+ flux.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the parameter exploration results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Most parameter changes led to small deviations from the predicted magnitudes of LTP/LTD.
source: As expected, most parameter changes led to small deviations from the predicted magnitudes of LTP/LTD (Figure 8, grey bars).
evidence: This is supported by the sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 8.

claim: Alterations of the initial concentration of 10 species and 12 reaction rates resulted in a notable (>15%) amplification or attenuation of LTD or LTP.
source: Alterations of the initial concentration of a number of species (10 out of 47) and reaction rates (12 out of 223) resulted in a notable (>15%) amplification or attenuation of LTD (Figure 8A) or LTP (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by the sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: None of the parameter changes completely abolished the LTP or LTD.
source: Importantly, none of the parameter changes completely abolished the LTP or LTD.
evidence: This is based on the sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The model is robust to small alterations in initial concentrations and reaction rates.
source: Taken together, our model is robust to small alterations in initial concentrations and reaction rates, but parameters influencing the Ca2+ dynamics, GluR1 activity, or the PKA-pathway signalling can have relatively large effects on the model output.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The model can be flexibly tuned to reproduce data from the experimental literature of cortical LTP/LTD through the use of varying concentrations of different proteins.
source: Here, we show that our model for intracellular signalling in a cortical post-synaptic spine — through the use of varying concentrations of different proteins — can be flexibly tuned to reproduce data from the experimental literature of cortical LTP/LTD.
evidence: This is supported by the model fitting results shown in Figure 9.

claim: The model found groups of parameter sets that fit within one standard deviation on average from the target values of synaptic conductance for each data set.
source: We found groups of parameter sets that fit within one standard deviation (SD) on average from the target values of synaptic conductance for each data set of Table 2 (Figure 9A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the model fitting results shown in Figure 9A-C.

claim: The data sets EC-1 and BC were particularly challenging to fit (<0.2% of the parameter sets tested by the optimiser gave an acceptable fit).
source: The data sets EC-1 and BC were particularly challenging to fit (<0.2% of the parameter sets tested by the optimiser gave an acceptable fit; Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by the model fitting results shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The data set AuC-2 was the easiest to fit (3.9% of the parameter sets were acceptable).
source: By contrast, the data set AuC-2 was the easiest to fit (3.9% of the parameter sets were acceptable; Figure 9D).
evidence: This is supported by the model fitting results shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The GluR1 ratio was significantly larger in the model parameters fitted to the data from LTP-expressing neurons than from LTD-expressing neurons.
source: As a contrasting example, our model predicts a large variety of parameters that reproduce the LTP and LTD of data sets AuC-1 and AuC-2 but, consistent with the results of Figure 7, the GluR1 ratio was significantly larger in the model parameters fitted to the data from LTP-expressing neurons than from LTD-expressing neurons (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is supported by the model fitting results shown in Figure 9E and statistical testing.

claim: The inhibition of CaMKII impaired the LTP in data set EC-1 (horizontal pathway) but had little or no effect on the plasticity in other cortical areas.
source: The inhibition of CaMKII impaired the LTP in data set EC-1 (horizontal pathway) but had little or no effect on the plasticity in other cortical areas (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The lack of effect of CaMKII blockade on the ascending pathway of EC validates the underlying models since similar results were observed in Ma et al., 2008.
source: The lack of effect of CaMKII blockade on the ascending pathway of EC — an experiment which was not included in the fitting of the model (Table 2) — validates the underlying models in this aspect since similar results were observed in Ma et al., 2008.
evidence: This is a validation of the model predictions against experimental data not used in fitting.

claim: The inhibition of PKA impaired LTP in all cortical areas, except for LTP in the horizontal pathway of the EC (EC-1).
source: The inhibition of PKA impaired LTP in all cortical areas, except for LTP in the horizontal pathway of the EC (EC-1; Figure 10C).
evidence: This is supported by the simulation results shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The models predicted that LTP of the CC→PFC pathway and LFS-induced LTP in VC can be effectively weakened or even be transformed to a mild LTD by PKA blockade.
source: Our models also predicted that LTP of the CC→PFC pathway and LFS-induced LTP in VC can be effectively weakened or even be transformed to a mild LTD by PKA blockade (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the simulation results shown in Figure 10C.

claim: The models predicted that PKC inhibition transformed all forms of LTD (LFS-induced LTD in VC-1 and VC-2; LTD in AuC-2) into LTP and impaired certain forms of LTP (LTP in EC-2; LTP in AuC-1).
source: Finally, our models predicted that PKC inhibition transformed all forms of LTD (LFS-induced LTD in VC-1 and VC-2; LTD in AuC-2) into LTP and impaired certain forms of LTP (LTP in EC-2; LTP in AuC-1) (Figure 10D).
evidence: This is a prediction based on the simulation results shown in Figure 10D.

claim: Almost all forms of post-synaptic plasticity in the cortex are likely to be PKA-dependent.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that almost all forms of post-synaptic plasticity in the cortex are likely to be PKA-dependent, and that many types of cortical plasticity are also influenced by CaMKII and PKC activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 10.

claim: Many types of cortical plasticity are also influenced by CaMKII and PKC activity.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that almost all forms of post-synaptic plasticity in the cortex are likely to be PKA-dependent, and that many types of cortical plasticity are also influenced by CaMKII and PKC activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results shown in Figure 10.

claim: GluR2 subunits are highly expressed in neocortical neurons.
source: GluR2 subunits are highly expressed in neocortical neurons (Kondo et al., 1997), and their endocytosis mediates (or, at minimum, is correlated with) synaptic depression in many cortical regions such as ACC (Toyoda et al., 2007), VC (Heynen et al., 2003), and PFC (Van den Oever et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: GluR2 endocytosis mediates (or is correlated with) synaptic depression in many cortical regions such as ACC, VC, and PFC.
source: GluR2 subunits are highly expressed in neocortical neurons (Kondo et al., 1997), and their endocytosis mediates (or, at minimum, is correlated with) synaptic depression in many cortical regions such as ACC (Toyoda et al., 2007), VC (Heynen et al., 2003), and PFC (Van den Oever et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Previous intracellular signalling-based models of neocortical LTP/LTD do not take into account the contributions of GluR2 subunit.
source: Previous intracellular signalling-based models of neocortical LTP/LTD exist, but they do not take into account the contributions of GluR2 subunit.
evidence: This is an assessment of the limitations of previous models based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: There is support for the order of events where LTD is caused by modest Ca2+ inputs that lead to PP1 or PP2B-mediated dephosphorylation of S845.
source: Although there is support for this order of events (Lee and Kirkwood, 2011; Diering et al., 2016), newer findings have confirmed the low degrees of phosphorylation of both S831 and S845 at a basal state in cortical cells, especially in synaptic spines (Diering et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Newer findings have confirmed the low degrees of phosphorylation of both S831 and S845 at a basal state in cortical cells, especially in synaptic spines.
source: Although there is support for this order of events (Lee and Kirkwood, 2011; Diering et al., 2016), newer findings have confirmed the low degrees of phosphorylation of both S831 and S845 at a basal state in cortical cells, especially in synaptic spines (Diering et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an experimental study.

claim: The model can be used to explain some of the discrepancies in the experimental data regarding the diversity of LTP/LTD observed across cell types in the brain.
source: A key challenge in the study of synaptic plasticity is the diversity of LTP/LTD observed across the cell types in the brain (Granger and Nicoll, 2014). Differences in the transcriptome have been proposed as one of the sources for this variability (Lisachev and Shtark, 2018). We believe our model can be used to explain some of the discrepancies in the experimental data in this regard and expand the understanding of possible molecular contributors to LTP/LTD.
evidence: This is a prospective claim about the utility of the model.

claim: Activation of PKA pathway by dopamine or noradrenaline in PFC pyramidal neurons increases the synaptic conductance through GluR1 membrane insertion.
source: For example, it is known that activation of PKA pathway by dopamine or noradrenaline in PFC pyramidal neurons increases the synaptic conductance through GluR1 membrane insertion (Sun et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The model proposes that LTP can be impaired by over- or underexpression of many involved proteins, such as AC1, I-1, PDE4, PDE1, GluR1, and CaM, and even alterations in ATP concentration.
source: Our model is in agreement with this (Figure 3), but it also proposes that the LTP can be impaired by over- or underexpression of many involved proteins, such as AC1, I-1 (inhibitor of PP1), PDE4, PDE1, GluR1, and CaM, and even alterations in ATP concentration (see Figure 8B).
evidence: This is based on the sensitivity analysis results shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The model suggests that the plasticity outcome of the STDP protocol is strongly correlated with the total amount of Ca2+ entering the post-synaptic spine.
source: Due to the inclusion of three major LTP/LTD pathways in the neocortex, our model provides a more accurate means than earlier models for exploring how the Ca2+ dynamics in the spine affects the plasticity outcome in many stimulation protocols, STDP in particular. Our model suggests that the plasticity outcome of the STDP protocol is strongly correlated with the total amount of Ca2+ entering the post-synaptic spine, and less so with the peak Ca2+ flux (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The total amount of Ca2+ influx could provide a better biomarker for plasticity than the previously considered amplitude and duration of the Ca2+ transient.
source: The total amount of Ca2+ influx could thus provide a better biomarker for plasticity than the previously considered amplitude and duration of the Ca2+ transient (Evans and Blackwell, 2015).
evidence: This is a prospective claim based on the model results and comparison with previous work.
